scene: Inferno XIV — fiery rain on burning sand; Capaneus defies
story: After the wood, Dante and Virgil reach a desert of hot, sterile sand, with flakes of fire raining continuously from above.
Different groups of punished souls lie, sit, or run upon the burning ground; Dante sees one gigantic figure lying unyielding beneath the flames.
Dante asks about the figure. Capaneus names himself and continues his defiance of Jupiter even while suffering.
Virgil rebukes Capaneus, saying that his unquenched pride compounds his punishment.
The travelers continue beside a small red stream that crosses the sand; the water and banks resist the flames and provide a path.
Virgil begins to explain the origins of the rivers of Hell through the Old Man of Crete; the detailed river genealogy is held for the next stage.
